chapter_theme: The poet describes the kingdom's capital from outside in: its people's refusal of the courtesan's snare, then groves, ponds, elephant enclosures and arenas, training grounds, crowded and gilded streets, the moat and the cloud-clasped wall, ending in a catalogue of the war engines on the wall. No character acts; the city is built up as abundant, pleasure-filled and, at its edge, armed.

78.reading: The poet announces that he will describe the noble, fragrant capital, whose people stand high in worth because they are not caught in the net of women whose eyes trap lustful men like beasts, keep the flesh of their wealth and throw away the body.
78.nuance: The city is praised first for what its men refuse. The hunting figure is exact: the lustful are the game (மா), the eye is the net, wealth is the meat kept (தசை தழீஇ) and the man is the carcass let go (உடலம் விட்டிடும்). The city is not named in these verses.

claims.claim: women who sell love trap lustful men with their eyes, take their wealth and cast the men off, and worth lies in not being caught

79.reading: Groves surround the city, where champak branches reaching the sky bend with blossom, bees burrow in the flowers and scatter pollen, and koels and peacocks call back and forth in a shade that holds the eye.

80.reading: The city's ponds, thick with the sandal paste, garlands, body powder, incense, oil and saffron washed off the bathers, look as if covered with a cloth of flowers.

81.reading: Around the stone wall, set at its foot with iron posts, lie the enclosures where great tuskers come in with their cow elephants, drawn by sugarcane and sheaves of ripe paddy.
81.nuance: வாரி is taken here as the elephant enclosure or stall; if it means the pits or traps where wild elephants are caught, the verse describes their capture rather than their keeping.

82.reading: There are arenas fit for elephant fights, where tuskers streaming musth from three places drive their killing tusks into each other like two mountains clashing.

83.reading: Long rows of workshops stand where craftsmen saw the pearl-bearing white tusks and fit them with patterned caps set with diamonds.

84.reading: Together lie the chariot courses where gold dust flies from the wheels, the circuits for garlanded horses, the grounds for sword and shield and the grounds for the curved bow.

85.reading: Past the working quarters of the outer town, the drums of the inner outskirts sound like a sea that has burst, and the crowd there is like that sea held behind a sluice.
85.nuance: The two halves of the sea simile split sound from mass: the drums are the sea breaking loose, the people the same sea penned in.

86.reading: The streets, where women spray vermilion and gold powder mixed with sandal water from balls and squirts, lie on the ground like a rainbow.

87.reading: Gem-studded pots set in rows on the tops of golden mansions look like flocks of peacocks perched on flowering vengai trees, longing for the rain clouds.

88.reading: The shadow of the long banners strokes the moon's brow, and the clouds, sweating and roaring in rage, tremble and drop on the mansion tops, where they run down as falls and seem to weep.
88.nuance: A comic conceit: the clouds are jealous of the banners that touch the moon, and their rain is recast as tears of defeat.

89.reading: Children ride little golden carts topped with golden elephants, and the bright earrings that frightened women fling at the fowl lie so thick that the carts' wheels cannot turn.
89.nuance: Wealth is shown by its waste: gold ear ornaments are thrown like stones and clog the streets.

90.reading: Garlands and gold mingle where women with brows bent like bows mix with spear-bearing men, so that one wonders whether this is the dwelling of the gods.

91.reading: When the strong-shouldered young men in their desire seize the fine silk garment, the women in shame put out the lamp with a throw of gold powder, and the powder rises and drifts out over the outskirts.
91.nuance: The verse turns a bedroom moment into a measure of the city's wealth: so many lamps are put out with gold dust that it spills beyond the walls. The play on சுணம் (powder, also the fine weave of the silk) runs through every line.

92.reading: Coconuts knocked down by the pestles of women pounding musk fall to the ground, and the startled peacocks fly off to dance on the tall masts of ships.
92.nuance: The masts place the city beside a harbour or navigable water, which the verse gives only in passing.

93.reading: So crowded is the rich city with people of the eighteen tongues that a sesame seed let fall would not reach the ground, and it looks like a fruit tree full of birds.
93.nuance: மூவறு பாடை (thrice six languages) is the conventional count of the world's speeches; the claim is that every people trades or lives here.

94.reading: The poet announces that he will describe the moat, full of open lotuses, which the women with pearl strings and spear-like eyes call the nest of the green parrots they carry on their wrists.
94.nuance: The lines are hard to construe: the parrots' young (பார்ப்பு) may be said to be the lotuses, or the women may tell the parrots the moat is their home; the verse in any case moves from the women of the streets to the moat.

95.reading: In the moat, schools of seizing sharks and heaps of crocodiles roam without catching any man, and when the big prawns that leap in fear churn the cold water, flocks of birds rise and cry.
95.nuance: The predators find no prey: no one falls into the moat, which is the moat's success as a defence.

96.reading: A drake swan that has quarrelled with its mate leaves the flock and settles alone in a lotus while the bees hum, like an ascetic who withdraws from company and strives in yoga to be rid of stain.
96.nuance: The simile sets a lover's sulk beside an ascetic's withdrawal, and the joke cuts both ways. கறை அற (to be free of stain) fits the Jain picture of the soul cleansed of karmic matter, but the verse names no doctrine.

97.reading: At the lovely bathing ghats of the moat no black vessel is ever dipped, only gold, silver and gems, and the saffron washed from the women's young breasts feasts the water till it turns red.

98.reading: The moat is a courtesan in that it destroys those who fall into it, with its wide expanse for hips and red water for a mouth; but with flowers opening on it like a bride, it is otherwise a lovely maiden held under strict guard.
98.nuance: The courtesan of verse 78, whom the citizens refuse, returns as the image of the moat's threat to an enemy; the guarded maiden gives its inaccessibility. The syntax of lines 1 and 3 is compressed and the split between the two comparisons is a reading.

99.reading: The spathes of the fragrant areca, opening like strings of pearls, and the honeyed blue lilies flowering in the moat spread their scent for a yojana, it is said.

100.reading: The poet turns to the high wall, whose top, forever wet, is clasped by clouds as a baby clings to its mother's breast and as mist hugs a great hill.
100.nuance: The two similes of embrace make the wall's height tender rather than menacing, just before the catalogue of its weapons.

101.reading: If enemy armies storm the wall, it has engines that hurl the hundred-killer, fearsome demon-elephants, great snakes that swallow, death-like vultures, lances and seizing beasts, the list continuing into the next verse.
101.nuance: These are machines named after what they do, not living creatures: நூற்றுவரைக் கொல்லி renders the weapon that kills a hundred at once. Line 4 has no finite verb; the catalogue runs on into verse 102, outside this chapter.

links.note: Both picture the bought embrace through a body: the Kural's woman of wealth embraces a stranger's corpse (பிணந்தழீஇ); the epic's net-woman embraces the flesh of wealth (தசை தழீஇ) and throws the body away.
links.teaches: Set beside the epic's hunter who keeps the meat of wealth and drops the carcass, the couplet's corpse reads naturally as the client handled by the woman, so the disgust in Kural 913 belongs to the trade itself rather than only to the man.

gains.a: the epic's hunting conceit is seen reworking the Kural's own corpse image and verb of embrace
gains.b: the couplet's disputed embracer gains a later poet's figure in which the woman is plainly the one who embraces and the man is the discarded body

links.note: The courtesan who ruins whoever falls into her net, refused by the citizens in 78, returns in 98 as the moat that ruins whoever falls into it.
links.teaches: The vice the poet praises the city for shunning becomes, twenty verses later, the figure of its defence, so the same destroying woman is a danger to citizens and a weapon against enemies.

links.note: The epic arms the wall with self-acting engines and names no defender; the Kural says every excellence of a fort is nothing without men excellent in action.
links.teaches: The epic's picture of a wall that fights by its own machinery is exactly the kind of fort the couplet calls empty, so the Kural supplies the missing term by which this lavish security can fail.

gains.a: the catalogue of engines gains a standard that shows what it leaves out: the people who must work them
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed excellences of a fort gain a concrete inventory of what a later poet thought those excellences were

source_issues: Verse 90 line 1 prints பொ(ன்)னும் with an editorial bracket for the restored letter.
Verse 101 has no finite verb in line 4; its list of war engines continues into verse 102, so the sentence crosses the chapter boundary (chapter 6 begins at 102).
